opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Distribution shift has become my main lens for a simple reason: a benchmark number tells you how a model does on one particular sample of data, collected in one particular way. What we actually care about is whether the model has learned the *task*, the underlying skill that benchmark is meant to stand in for. Distribution shift is how you pull those two apart.

If a model has really learned to, say, recognize objects or answer questions about a passage, its performance should hold up reasonably well when you change things that shouldn't matter: the lighting, the background, the phrasing, the source of the data. If performance collapses under those shifts, that's a strong signal the model latched onto shortcuts, spurious correlations that happened to be predictive in the training and test sets but have nothing to do with the task. The classic example is a classifier that's really using the background, like water for boats or grass for cows, rather than the object itself.

So in my work, shifts serve as a kind of stress test. You construct or collect data where the incidental features change but the task stays the same, and you see what breaks. That tells you much more about what the model has actually learned than another decimal point on an in-distribution leaderboard.

One thing that's come out of this line of research, from us and many others, is a surprisingly strong relationship between in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy. Across many models, they often fall roughly on a line. That's both encouraging and sobering. Encouraging, because better models do tend to be more robust. Sobering, because a lot of methods that claim to improve robustness are really just improving accuracy overall, and don't move you off that line. So a big part of what we try to do is ask what actually changes that relationship. Interventions like pretraining on large, diverse data seem to help, and we've also studied how fine-tuning choices can preserve or destroy robustness a pretrained model already has.

With today's large foundation models it gets even more interesting, because the very notion of "in-distribution" gets blurry. These models were trained on so much of the internet that it's hard to say what's novel to them. That makes careful thinking about shift more important, not less. If we want to claim a model can reason, or code, or do math, we need to evaluate it in ways that rule out "it saw something very close to this before." Distribution shift gives us the vocabulary and the tools to ask that question rigorously.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark scores reflect performance on a particular sample and discusses shortcuts, but it does not state that substantial compute on benchmark-like training data can produce strong benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: It presents shifts in incidental features while keeping the task constant as a stress test for whether a model learned the intended task, beyond its benchmark score.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a benchmark is really a proxy. We care about some underlying capability, say reading comprehension or recognizing objects, and the benchmark is a specific sample of inputs we've drawn from the world to measure it. When a model scores well, we'd like to conclude it has the capability. But there are two very different ways to score well. One is to actually solve the task in the way we intended. The other is to latch onto whatever regularities happen to be present in that particular dataset, things like spurious correlations, annotation artifacts, or just the specific style of how the examples were collected.

From inside the benchmark alone, those two are indistinguishable. Test accuracy on the same distribution can't tell them apart, because by construction the shortcuts work on the test set too. So the way I use distribution shift is as a lever to pull them apart. If I take the same task but change something that shouldn't matter for the underlying capability, a different image background, a different source of text, a different time period, a different population of annotators, then a model that truly solved the task should be fine, and a model that learned the artifacts should break. The size and shape of that drop under shift is the signal I'm after. It's a way of asking, did you learn what we thought we were measuring, or did you learn the dataset?

What I find really interesting is that this reframes a lot of questions. Instead of asking whether a model is good, I ask under which shifts it stays good and under which it fails, and what that tells us about what it has internalized. Sometimes the failures are predictable from in-distribution accuracy, and sometimes they aren't, and those cases where accuracy on the benchmark and robustness under shift come apart are exactly where the benchmark was lying to us about what was being solved. So distribution shift, for me, is less a nuisance to engineer around and more a diagnostic tool for understanding what the model actually learned.

r001.rationale: The response describes benchmark performance and dataset shortcuts, but does not say that training on benchmark-like data with substantial compute can produce strong scores.

r002.rationale: It proposes changing task-irrelevant conditions—such as image backgrounds or text sources—and using performance drops to distinguish solving the intended task from learning dataset artifacts.

astra-6.text:
I think of distribution shifts as a way to probe what a model has actually learned. When we evaluate on a benchmark, the training and test data often come from the same distribution. So doing well on that test set tells us something, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us whether the model has learned the underlying task or found a correlation that happens to be predictive in that dataset.

For example, if you’re trying to recognize an object, the background might be a useful predictor in your training data. You can get good test accuracy by using that background without learning to recognize the object in the way we intended. If we change the relationship between the object and the background, we can start to distinguish those possibilities.

So the question becomes: What changes should a model be able to handle if it has actually learned the task? We don’t expect it to work under every possible distribution shift. But by choosing shifts that preserve what we want the model to do while changing other aspects of the data, we can make that question more concrete. That gives us a way to study the gap between doing well on a benchmark and having the capability we hoped the benchmark was measuring.

r001.rationale: It says training and test data often share a distribution and that benchmark performance can be strong, but does not mention substantial compute.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing shifts that preserve the intended task, but does not specify slight, deployment-relevant shifts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of distribution shift as a way to probe what a model has actually learned. When we evaluate on a benchmark, the training and test data often come from essentially the same distribution. So good test performance tells us that the model generalizes within that distribution, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us that it solves the task in the way we intended.

For example, suppose we want a model to recognize cows, but most of the cows in the training data appear on grass. It could rely on the background instead of the animal. On a test set with the same correlation, that can look like a successful solution. If we change the background, we can start to distinguish those possibilities.

That’s the role distribution shifts play in how I frame the question: what can we change while keeping the underlying task the same, and does the model still work? A failure gives us evidence about which features or assumptions its success depended on. The challenge is then to understand which shifts we should expect a model to handle, and how to build models whose performance survives those changes.

r001.rationale: The response says training and test data often share a distribution and that this can yield good test performance, but it does not mention substantial compute.

r002.rationale: The response frames distribution shifts as a way to test whether a model solves the intended task, but does not specify slight, deployment-relevant shifts.
